title: The balance between compactness and forecast accuracy of data-driven latent-space reduced-order models in controlled wake flows
abstract: Model-based active flow control requires predictive models that are accurate, stable and fast enough for real-time optimisation. In controlled wake flows, this is often achieved through reduced-order models (ROMs) that first compress high-dimensional velocity snapshots into a latent space and then learn a time-stepping predictor for the dynamics in the latent space. Here, we study how the choice of the spatial encoder affects the predictability of the resulting latent coordinates for wake flows under control inputs. Using two actuated two-dimensional wake configurations, a simplified truck wake and the fluidic pinball, we compare proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) against nonlinear convolutional autoencoders (CAEs) and two types of variational autoencoders for compression, and evaluate …
authors: Alberto Solera-Rico, Patricia García-Caspueñas, Carlos Sanmiguel Vila, Stefano Discetti

title: Wake transitions and scaling laws of a streamwise-rotating angular particle in an inertial flow
abstract: The wake dynamics and regime transitions of a streamwise-rotating angular particle in an inertial flow at moderate Reynolds numbers are investigated by particle-resolved direct numerical simulations, with particular focus on a rotating cube. We first identify the mechanisms of vortex generation on the front edges and the rear face, showing that rotation-induced vortex merging governs several key regime transitions. A previously unreported spearhead regime is uncovered, characterised by a helical near-wake and a steady filamentary far-wake structure. We demonstrate that it originates from the partial merging of edge vortices and the central rotation-induced vortex. Streamwise rotation is found to moderately stabilise the wake, and to induce a quadratic scaling of both the drag coefficient u…
authors: Guodong Gai, Olivier Simonin, Anthony Wachs

title: Linear-model-based estimation of turbulent fluctuations in compressible turbulent boundary layers
abstract: Linear-model-based estimation provides an equation-based route to reconstruct turbulent fluctuations from limited measurements, but its performance in compressible turbulent boundary layers depends critically on both the inter-layer coherence and the modelling of nonlinear forcing. This study systematically extends and assesses linear-model-based estimation for velocity and temperature fluctuations in compressible turbulent boundary layers, using a logarithmic-region measurement plane at Mach numbers upper M equals 2 M = 2 $M=2$ , 4 and 6 under both adiabatic- and cold-wall conditions. With the direct numerical simulation databases, the linear coherence spectra are first analysed. Results show that the recoverable information is mainly confined to large scales especially when the estimatio…
authors: Yitong Fan, Hong Liu, Weipeng Li

title: Aggregation, breakup and size-dependent transport in a turbulent channel flow with cohesive particles
abstract: Due to attractive inter-particle forces, cohesive particles suspended in turbulence undergo a complex process of aggregation, breakup and restructuring. Despite a growing body of knowledge on the `flocculation’ of cohesive granular materials suspended in homogeneous isotropic turbulence, little focus has so far been placed on wall-bounded flows where turbulence and shear are inhomogeneous. This study presents a first investigation of a fully developed wall-bounded flow of resolved cohesive particles. Five direct numerical simulations of turbulent channel flows laden with finite-sized particles at successively increasing cohesive strength are performed. A population balance equation (PBE) framework is used to analyse aggregate dynamics. When integrated over the full domain, the PBE is close…
authors: Alexandre Leonelli, Lukas Widmer, Eckart Heinz Meiburg

title: A body-forcing model for heat transfer in rough-wall turbulent channel flow
abstract: A body-forcing strategy is proposed to model the effects of surface roughness on heat transfer in a turbulent flow. The model introduces a source term into the temperature transport equation that depends on a characteristic velocity scale, the local wall-relative temperature and the roughness density. We test it in direct numerical simulation (DNS) of a turbulent open channel at a constant Prandtl number of 0.71, and through extensive comparison with roughness-resolved DNS data, we show that the instantaneous local friction velocity is the appropriate velocity scale. Despite its simple formulation, it accurately captures the salient physics of rough-wall heat transfer, such as the breakdown of the Reynolds analogy, the characteristic plateau of the temperature roughness function and the fu…
authors: Krishna Reddy Maryada, Stuart Edward Norris, Daniel Chung, Michael MacDonald

title: Turbulence generation and data assimilation in wall-bounded flows with a latent diffusion model
abstract: Wall-bounded turbulent flows are chaotic and multiscale, rendering fast prediction at high Reynolds numbers computationally prohibitive in applications such as wind farms. Classical data assimilation is based on repeated solutions of the governing equations and, thus, inherits this cost. Generative models learn the probability distribution of flow states, enabling scalable probabilistic reconstruction. Our generative framework couples a variational autoencoder with a diffusion transformer to generate four-dimensional spatiotemporal samples. Bayesian conditioning enables data assimilation without retraining and allows statistical constraints to be imposed through sampling. The framework is applied to a subdomain of turbulent plane Couette flow, where the corresponding direct numerical simul…
authors: Fabian Steinbrenner, Baris Turan, Hao Teng, Heng Xiao

title: Bifurcation of laterally unconstrained flexible filaments in an inclined flow
abstract: The dynamics of laterally unconstrained flexible filaments in an inclined uniform flow is investigated numerically, inspired by the self-propelled behaviour of droplets and filaments in a crosswind. It is found that in addition to conventional downwind drifting, the filament can also undergo counterintuitive upwind motion, arising from a supercritical pitchfork bifurcation. Depending on the Reynolds number, bending stiffness and inflow inclination angle, the filament exhibits multiple wake and motion states, including static, quasi-static, vibrational and translational modes. In the reference frame translating laterally with the incoming flow, the upwind and downwind drifting states induced by different initial perturbations form a pair of dynamically equivalent, symmetry-related branches.…
authors: Kui Liu, Meng-Fan Xu, An-Kang Gao, Xi-Yun Lu

title: Scaling law for ventilated air layers modulated by superhydrophobic grooves
abstract: An innovative air-layer establishment method is developed and experimentally investigated, where superhydrophobic transverse grooves are introduced to modulate localised minimal-flux ventilation. The results demonstrate that, owing to the modulation by the transverse grooves, the characteristics of multiphase flow undergo a fundamental transition from discrete bubbles to a continuous air layer. This modulation is strictly governed by both the free-stream velocity and the groove size, expressed as Reynolds number ( italic Re Subscript upper D Re D $\textit{Re}_D$ ) and dimensionless groove size ( delta Superscript asterisk δ ∗ $\delta ^*$ ), respectively. title: Stability boundary prediction of nonlinear transonic buffet via a time-varying modelling method
abstract: Transonic shock buffet is a typical flow instability induced by shock-wave/boundary-layer interaction. It exhibits sustained shock oscillations and lift fluctuations, thereby restricting the flight envelope of aircraft. Previous numerical studies have revealed that evident hysteresis envelopes exist between the onset and extinction boundaries of transonic buffet during angle-of-attack sweeps. Hence accurate characterisation of buffet boundaries under representative dynamic manoeuvres is critical for assessing flight safety and expanding the flight envelope. In this study, a time-varying autoregressive with exogenous input model is established by integrating reduced-order and time-varying modelling to predict the buffet boundary under nonlinear transonic dynamic conditions. authors: Qiyue Ma, Xinyu Yang, Chuanqiang Gao

title: Relationships Between Aerosols, Warm Clouds, and Meteorological Factors Associated With Environmental Conditions Derived From Multiyear ARM Observations
abstract: Abstract We derive new aspects between clouds, aerosols, and meteorological factors using latest observations. We analyze multiyear measurements of atmospheric physical properties including warm clouds and aerosols collected at Atmospheric Radiation Measurement continental and maritime facilities during 2016–2020 and 2015–2021, respectively. Diurnal variation of the aerosol optical depth (AOD) collocated with a neighboring cloud results from adjacent low tropospheric vertical wind shear (VWS 725–925 hPa ) due to aerosols originating from soils stirred up by enhanced turbulence at Southern Great Plains (SGP). There are similarities between seasons (summer or winter) and surface wind directions (north or south) with respect to the relations between aerosol‐cloud, cloud‐cloud, and cloud‐meteo…
authors: Yoshihide Takano, Yu Gu, Yun Lin, Rong Fu et al.

title: Linear Versus Non‐linear Models in Predicting Low‐Cloud Regime Occurrences From Cloud‐Controlling Factors
abstract: Abstract Accurately predicting low‐cloud occurrences from environmental conditions is essential for reducing uncertainties in cloud‐climate feedbacks. This study evaluates linear and non‐linear frameworks—specifically, anomaly‐based ridge regression and neural network (NNet) that predict raw target values—to predict cloud regime occurrence frequencies from low‐cloud‐amount‐indices (LCAIs) and other cloud‐controlling factors at monthly, 4° resolution, using data from selected subtropical study regions. While the combined use of multiple LCAIs notably enhances linear model performance within the training domains, these models exhibit poor geographic transferability due to the diversity of cloud‐environment relationships. In contrast, an NNet model trained using raw physical variables consist…

title: How Does Terrain Relief of the Tibetan Plateau and the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau Individually Modulate Summer Regional Hourly Extreme Precipitation in the Sichuan Basin, China?
abstract: Abstract The influence of terrain relief over the Tibetan Plateau (TP) and the Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau on summer regional hourly extreme precipitation (RHEP) in the Sichuan Basin (SCB) under two dominant synoptic patterns remains poorly understood. Here, this study uses multi‐case Weather Research and Forecasting sensitivity experiments, in which the terrain relief of two plateaus is individually smoothed, to systematically investigate these modulation mechanisms. Terrain relief modulates low‐level flow and moisture, altering thermodynamic and dynamic processes of RHEP under different synoptic patterns. Under P1, featured by a westerly trough and a southwest vortex over western SCB, the terrain relief over the TP (Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau) prolongs the mean RHEP duration by 3.4 hr (0.6 hr) an…
authors: Xiaoke Xu, Anning Huang, Chunlei Gu, Yan Zhang

title: OceanTracker 0.5: fast adaptable Lagrangian particle  tracking in structured and unstructured grids
abstract: Particle tracking is frequently used to compute particle movements within hydrodynamic ocean models; however, modelling millions of particles is computationally challenging. OceanTracker is designed to reduce the time required to obtain results from particle tracking. Firstly, OceanTracker is computationally efficient, allowing users to simulate large numbers of particles in complex coastal environments, enabling improved statistics and exploration of a wider range of cases within acceptable run times. Secondly, OceanTracker can calculate multiple particle statistics during the computational run, eliminating the need to record and post-process large volumes of particle trajectories. The adaptability of OceanTracker's modular computational pipeline allows users to add and modify components …

title: Calibration guidelines and a runoff-isotope module  for lake proxy system modeling (PRYSM v2.0)
abstract: Lake sediments preserve information about past air temperature and precipitation, providing critical, real-world targets to validate climate models. However, these paleoclimate data encode information about multiple climate signals as well as lake dynamics, which makes comparison of paleoclimate data and model output challenging. Proxy system models (PSMs), or forward models that translate climate variables into proxy units, are tools for mechanistically interpreting paleoclimate data. PRYSM v2.0 is a PSM for paleoclimate data archived in lake sediments. Foundational to the accuracy of the PSM is a comprehensive understanding of the modern lake system supported by observations and meteorological inputs. However, two obstacles exist. First, stable oxygen and hydrogen isotope values in lake …
authors: Rebecca G. Topness, Elizabeth K. Thomas, Michaela Fendrock, Gerard A. Otiniano

title: GPU-accelerated three-dimensional variational data assimilation with automatic differentiation for WRF-Chem
abstract: This study developed a PyTorch-based three-dimensional variational (3DVar) data assimilation system (PY3DVar) for the Weather Research and Forecasting model coupled to Chemistry (WRF-Chem), which integrates automatic differentiation (AD) to replace traditional manual gradient derivation and adopts Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) acceleration for high computational efficiency. PY3DVar enables the simultaneous assimilation of gaseous pollutants (SO 2 , NO 2 , CO, O 3 ) and particulate matter (PM 2.5 , PM 10 ) and supports flexible deployment on both Central Processing Unit (CPU) and GPU computing platforms. Idealized tests were first conducted to verify the physical consistency of the assimilation system. Twenty consecutive real-case assimilation experiments, each followed by a 24 h forecast,…

title: Observed Characteristics and Formation Mechanisms of Record‐Low Western North Pacific Tropical Cyclone Landfalls Over China in Summer 2024
abstract: Abstract Summer 2024 observed a record‐low tropical cyclone (TC) landfall activity over China, with only two landfalls representing a 59.8% reduction from the 1979–2023 climatological mean. This study investigates the characteristics and underlying mechanisms of this extreme suppression, revealing distinct monthly variations driven by divergent genesis‐related factors. In June, no TCs formed, attributable to an anomalously strong and westward‐extended western Pacific subtropical high (WPSH) that suppressed monsoon trough‐associated convection. July recorded near‐normal landfall frequency despite moderately suppressed genesis, as westward‐displaced TC formations and southeasterly steering flows favored TC tracks toward southeastern China. title: Mid‐to‐High‐Latitude Air‐Sea Interactions Facilitate the Synchronization of the East Asian Winter Monsoon System Components
abstract: Abstract East Asian winter monsoon (EAWM) is a powerful circulation system that profoundly influences both regional and global climate. While extensive studies have explored the factors driving the EAWM variation, recent studies reveal that the EAWM is not always an integrated system, exhibiting a notable decoupling tendency in recent decades. This underscores the need to revisit the mechanisms changing the EAWM components' coherence from a hemispheric perspective. Focusing on the co‐variations between the two key EAWM components of East Asian trough (EAT) and Siberian High (SH), and combining the analyses on observations/reanalysis, atmospheric general circulation model simulations, and fully‐coupled climate model simulations, this study reveals that the in‐phase EAT‐SH variation primaril…
authors: Shui Yu, Jianqi Sun

title: The Impact of Aerosol on Liquid‐Ice Phase Transition and Precipitation Formation in Mixed‐Phase Clouds: A Case Study
abstract: Abstract This study investigates how aerosol perturbations influence precipitation formation in supercooled stratiform clouds with different supercooled liquid water content (SLWC). Numerical experiments are performed using the WRF‐SBM model with different concentrations of cloud condensation nuclei (CCN) and ice‐nucleating particle (IN) within the same cloud field. Two cloud systems with contrasting SLWC are identified under similar large‐scale environmental conditions. The results show that the two systems exhibit distinctly different responses to aerosol perturbations. In the low‐SLWC cloud system, precipitation is more sensitive to increased CCN. The enhancement of CCN leads to an increase in the concentration of cloud droplets and a suppression of collision‐coalescence processes. This…

title: The onset of Darcy–Forchheimer convection in an inclined porous medium with the temperature dependence of viscosity and anisotropic thermal diffusivity
abstract: This study investigates how the impact of an internal heat source and anisotropic thermal diffusivity influences convective motion in a horizontally inclined porous medium saturated with fluid, assuming an adiabatic bottom boundary and an isothermal top boundary. Here, the momentum equation is formulated using the Darcy–Forchheimer model and assumes that the viscosity is a linear function of the temperature. Linear and nonlinear stability analyses have been conducted to determine the stability by calculating the critical Rayleigh number and the associated wavenumber. title: Hydrodynamic forces in the drainage of an electrolyte confined between dielectric surfaces
abstract: We present a theory for the hydrodynamic forces in the drainage of an electrolyte film confined between charged curved surfaces, which applies to small gaps under local equilibrium across the film thickness. We derive a local Onsager formalism describing the coupled flow rate, charge and solute fluxes, which accounts for all degrees of overlap of the electrical double layers (EDLs) and can be adapted to a variety of electrical, chemical or hydrodynamic boundary conditions. We explore in detail the case of a monovalent electrolyte with constant surface charge and no-slip boundary conditions. title: Scalings of small-scale shear layers in temporally developing turbulent boundary layers
abstract: Small-scale shear layers in temporally developing turbulent boundary layers are investigated using direct numerical simulations at momentum-thickness Reynolds numbers from 2000 to 13 000. Flow statistics are evaluated in a local coordinate system aligned with each shear layer identified by the shear intensity. Conditional mean fields show that shear layers are embedded in a biaxial strain. Near the wall, these conditional fields further reveal two distinct regions of intense rigid-body rotation beneath the shear layer, leading to momentum transfer through a mechanism consistent with counter-rotating vortex pairs. title: Observation operator and detection limits for MODIS and VIIRS Fire Radiative Power products
abstract: We analyze the MODIS and VIIRS active-fire Fire Radiative Power (FRP) products, suggest an approximation for the FRP detection limit as a linear function of a pixel area, and develop analytical observation operators for both pixel-level and gridded FRP products. We have shown that the collection-6.1 of MODIS has the FRP detection limit at 3.7 MW in case of a nadir retrieval at a clear-sky night. For a daytime sideview, it reaches as high as 40 MW. For VIIRS, the smallest fire reliably detected at night is 0.5 MW. Application of the developed operators for the cross-mapping the MODIS and VIIRS datasets at the pixel/granule level confirmed their consistency. title: Bypass transition beneath internal solitary waves in turbulent boundary layers
abstract: Process-based studies of the transition to turbulence beneath internal solitary waves (ISWs) have typically assumed a laminar bottom boundary layer (BBL) and two-dimensional flow. In natural environments, however, ISWs often propagate over turbulent three-dimensional BBLs. title: Interannual Changes in Springtime Near‐Surface Wind Speed Over Eastern China Associated With the Nonlinear Combined Effects of Large‐Scale Circulation Changes
abstract: Abstract Near‐surface wind speed (NSWS) is a key meteorological variable regulating energy, water vapor, and momentum exchanges between the land surface and the planetary boundary layer. While long‐term trends and interdecadal variability of NSWS have been extensively investigated in China, the causes of its interannual variability remain insufficiently understood. This study conducts a analysis of springtime NSWS (NSWSspr) over eastern China during 1970–2020, identifies the underlying causes of its interannual change. Results indicate that NSWSspr exhibited a statistically robust quasi‐four‐year oscillation, and it was modulated by coordinated anomalies in large‐scale atmospheric circulations over the North Pacific, Northeast Asia, and the Northwest Pacific. title: Isotopic Compositions and Source Identification of Atmospheric Particulate Bound Cadmium in Chinese Megacities
abstract: Abstract Particulate matter (PM) bound cadmium (Cd) deposition on the Earth's surface poses significant ecological risks to humans and the environment. Cd stable isotopes are useful tracers for understanding sources and biogeochemical cycling in the Earth's ecosystems, yet knowledge of atmospheric Cd isotopic compositions remains limited. Here we present measurements of Cd isotopic compositions in fine particulate matter (PM 2.5 ) in five megacities selected to represent different anthropogenic Cd emission structures across China and explore potential atmospheric Cd sources. title: Strengthening of the Linkage Between the Stratospheric Polar Vortex and Winter Compound Cold‐Wet Events in the Yangtze River Basin After the Late 1990s
abstract: Abstract Based on the observational and reanalysis data for winters (December‐January‐February, DJF) of 1962–2022, this study addressed the relationship between the stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) and compound cold‐wet events (CCWEs) in the Yangtze River Basin (YRB). It is found that their relationship varies from an insignificant correlation to a significant negative correlation in the late 1990s. During the latter period, the winter SPV anomaly can excite an Atlantic‐Eurasian teleconnection wave train in the troposphere, which then triggers downstream responses. On one hand, the Siberian high intensifies and the polar front jet weakens, directing strong cold airs southward into the YRB. title: Inertial gravity currents released from a lock in frames under horizontal oscillations: Analytical model
abstract: We consider the flow of a gravity current released from a lock inside a tank which performs horizontal oscillations (equivalent to internal pressure-gradient pulses), in the buoyancy–inertia (high-Reynolds-number) regime. We develop a shallow-water model which provides clear-cut insights and simple predictions of the propagation, height and velocity fields as a function of time, for a wide range of parameters. Comparisons with the simulations of Bingol et al. (2025 J. Fluid. Mech. , vol. 1002, A14) support the approximate analysis. Moreover, we point out a new effect, called pulse-buoyancy, which was not covered by these simulation. title: Process-based upgrades to the WRF multi-layer green-roof scheme (WRF-MLGR v2.0) and evaluation against field observations
abstract: Green roofs can moderate urban heat by increasing latent heat flux and reducing sensible heat flux. However, capturing these effects in models depends on accurate representation of key green-roof processes, including substrate heat and moisture transport, soil-vegetation-atmosphere energy and moisture exchanges, interactions with the underlying roof, and drainage. Here we introduce targeted, process-based updates to the green-roof scheme (hereafter, MLGR) within the multi-layer urban canopy model (BEP-BEM) in the WRF mesoscale model to address key limitations in the original formulation. title: Intermittency and hibernation in elasto-inertial Taylor–Couette flow at moderate Reynolds number
abstract: We investigate the presence of intermittency, a well-known phenomenon in Newtonian turbulence, in viscoelastic Taylor–Couette flow at fixed inertia, (Reynolds number, italic Re Re $\textit {Re}$ = 120). Using particle image velocimetry measurements in the r–z plane for a broad range of elasticities, italic El El $\textit{El}$ = 0–0.64, we reveal a dual role of viscoelasticity, even at moderate italic Re Re $\textit {Re}$ : it can destabilise the flow and trigger turbulence at moderate elasticity but suppress turbulence intensity at higher values. abstract: A self-consistent saturation model for the prediction of aeroacoustic limit cycles emerging in turbulent low-Mach cavity flows (Reynolds number upper R e equals script upper O left parenthesis 10 Superscript 5 Baseline right parenthesis R e = O ( 10 5 ) $Re=\mathcal{O}(10^5)$ , Mach number upper M asymptotically equals 0.2 M ≃ 0.2 $M\simeq 0.2$ ) is proposed. title: Nonlinear regime of radially spreading extensional flows. Part 2. Power-law fluids
abstract: Radially spreading extensional flows can become unstable and develop tearing patterns consisting of rifts and tongues. Such patterns have been observed in laboratory experiments with strain-rate-softening (shear-thinning) polymer solutions and in spreading ice shelves. Linear stability analysis predicts that axisymmetric spreading of power-law fluids becomes unstable when the fluid is shear thinning. However, understanding the emergence and evolution of rifts requires analysis of the nonlinear flow regime. In Part 1 of this study we developed a numerical simulation of the full nonlinear equations and showed that Newtonian fluids remain globally stable, consistently with theoretical predictions and experimental observations. title: Spanwise flow correction model for blade element theory considering geometric effects by symbolic regression
abstract: The finite span and twist of wind turbine blades induce spanwise flow, along with a tip vortex. Conventional blade element theory, rooted in a two-dimensional assumption, cannot capture these spanwise effects. However, most existing three-dimensional (3-D) corrections neglect intrinsic geometric effects leading to inaccuracies near the tip and in non-rotating cases. To address this, we propose the 3-D geometric effects model incorporating axial and radial velocity factors (3-DGAR model), a physically consistent correction to blade element momentum theory. The model captures two fundamental phenomena: downwash that modifies the local effective angle of attack and tip pressure loss driven by radial velocity transport. A coherent physical pathway from the tip vortex to load reduction is estab…

title: Distributed roughness-induced transition on a blunt body at Mach 6: a numerical investigation
abstract: Surface roughness significantly impacts transition to turbulence, especially over high-speed, blunt geometries where surface ablation is necessary to mitigate heat loads during atmospheric entry. Inspired by sand-grain roughness experiments performed by Hollis (2017), we perform the first direct numerical simulation of a blunt cylinder in Mach 6 cross-flow with roughness elements distributed along the entire surface. Such simulations aimed to uncover the precise means by which laminar–turbulent transition occurs given the limited measurements attainable from experiments and non-existent high-fidelity simulations. title: Flow in a narrow-gap annulus: drag reduction by inner cylinder azimuthal oscillation
abstract: The axial flow through a thin gap between two concentric cylinders is investigated using direct numerical simulation (DNS) of the Navier–Stokes equations. It is shown that by imposing a stationary, harmonic, azimuthal velocity at the inner cylinder wall, drag reduction is always attained while power saving is limited to a portion of the explored amplitude–axial wavelength space. The largest values of drag reduction and power saving are 44 percent sign 44 % $44\,\%$ and 11 percent sign 11 % $11\,\%$ , respectively, obtained for different amplitude–axial wavelength pairs. title: On the spatio-temporal dynamics of turbulent flow separation over a fence with a splitter plate in uniform flow
abstract: The spatial and temporal dynamics of separated flow induced by a fence with a splitter plate in uniform flow at moderate Reynolds numbers were investigated using time-resolved particle image velocimetry. The Reynolds numbers, based on the free-stream velocity and the fence height above the splitter plate, were 2700, 5500 and 7500. The mean separated flow is characterised by a large primary clockwise recirculating vortex above the splitter plate and a smaller counter-rotating secondary vortex in the corner of the fence and splitter plate. Guided by different vorticity thickness growth rates, the separated shear layer is partitioned into four regions, whose dynamics are governed by the initial roll-up, shear layer stabilisation, wall-induced large-scale vortex breakdown and post-reattachment…
authors: Jinhao Kang, Mark Francis Tachie

title: Stratospheric Circulation in the Southern Hemisphere: Links to Tropical Winds, Ozone, and the Hunga Eruption—Part 1: Evidence From ERA5 Reanalysis
abstract: Abstract The interannual variability of the Southern Hemisphere polar vortex plays a key role in ozone depletion and recovery but this variability and its teleconnection patterns are less understood than in the Northern Hemisphere. Using ERA5 reanalysis data from 1980 to 2022 (43 years), we studied the variability of the Southern Hemisphere vortex by focusing on the location of the winter jet maximum in the upper stratosphere (1 hPa). We identify two dominant modes: In the first one, the core of the jet at 1 hPa remains at lower latitudes (40°S–50°S, LLJ) throughout austral winter (9 years, including 2022 following the Hunga eruption). title: Water Vapor Transport Mechanisms During the Henan ‘7.20’ Extreme Rainfall Event Inferred From GNSS, ERA5, and GDAS1 Data
abstract: Abstract The processes linking remote moisture supply to extreme inland rainfall remain insufficiently quantified. This study integrates high‐frequency Global Navigation Satellite System‐derived Precipitable water vapor (PWV) (GNSS‐derived PWV), radiosonde observations, ERA5 reanalysis, a four‐boundary moisture budget, HYSPLIT trajectories, and moist potential vorticity diagnostics for the July 2021 Henan extreme rainfall event. GNSS and ERA5 capture similar regional moisture evolution, while GNSS resolves sharper station‐scale variations. Absolute PWV has its strongest regional correlation with subsequent rainfall at a 7‐hr lead, whereas the 3‐hr PWV change identifies a 2–6 hr precursor window, with maximum correlation at 4 hr. title: Tidal Variability in the Lower Thermosphere: Relative Importance of ENSO, QBO, PJO, MJO, and Ly α
abstract: Abstract Atmospheric tides in the lower thermosphere play an important role in regulating upper‐atmospheric conditions relevant to space weather. However, their spatial and temporal variability remains poorly understood, apart from seasonal variations. Previous studies have shown that tides can be influenced by meteorological and solar conditions. This study clarifies the relative importance of the El Niño‐Southern Oscillation (ENSO), the Quasi‐Biennial Oscillation (QBO), the Northern and Southern Polar‐night Jet Oscillations (NPJO and SPJO), the Madden‐Julian Oscillation (MJO), and Lyman‐alpha (Ly) radiation to tidal variability in the lower thermosphere. title: Stratospheric Circulation in the Southern Hemisphere: Links to Tropical Winds, Ozone and the Hunga Eruption—Part II: Evidence From a Global Chemistry‐Climate Model
abstract: Abstract The Southern Hemisphere (SH) stratospheric circulation can be categorized based upon the development of a Low‐Latitude Jet (LLJ) in the upper stratosphere during winter months. We analyze the dynamics of the LLJ based on a large ensemble of chemistry‐climate model simulations, supported by reanalysis data. The LLJ is associated with westerly wind anomalies in the middle and upper stratosphere during mid‐winter, coupled with weak planetary wave activity and a slower Brewer‐Dobson circulation. Circulation effects extend into the tropical upper stratosphere, where the LLJ impacts the tropical semi‐annual oscillation (SAO). Additionally, the LLJ is linked to a persistent, strong polar vortex in the lower stratosphere during October–December. This cold, strong vortex is associated with…

title: Weakened Variability of Afro‐Asian Monsoonal Precipitation in Response to a Past Warm‐Cold Transition
abstract: Abstract The Afro‐Asian monsoon domain faces a “wetter and more variable” paradigm under future warming, but whether a “drier and less variable” hydroclimate emerges under cooling remains unconstrained. Using a ∼1° transient global climate simulation during the Last Interglacial (130–115 ka) covering the precession‐induced warm‐cold transition, we demonstrate a general weakening trend of precipitation variability over the Afro‐Asian monsoon domain except for southern India at multiple timescales, but with divergent dynamical mechanisms. Precipitation variability changes are dynamically dominated by the vertical motion variability over the Asian monsoon domain associated with diabatic heating, while thermodynamically controlled by cooling‐induced reduced atmospheric moisture over West Afric…

title: Fast and slow surfactants in turbulence-driven bubble breakup
abstract: When a large air cavity breaks in a turbulent flow, it goes through very large deformations and cascading events of new interface formation, including elongated filaments and bubbles over a wide range of scales, with their rate of formation controlled by turbulence and capillary processes. We experimentally investigate the effects of surfactants and salt on the fragmentation of a large air cavity, and observe a fivefold increase of the number of bubbles being produced in some cases. We characterise the bubble size distribution resulting from successive breakups in such a transient configuration. title: Diffusion-driven flow about an impermeable sphere or cylinder in a stably stratified liquid: the singular limit of small Rayleigh numbers
abstract: When an impermeable spherical particle is suspended in stably stratified ambient salinity gradient, the curving of the constant-density surfaces gives rise to non-conservative body forces which cannot be supported by pressure gradients. As a result, fluid motion is engendered. Considering small particles, we here address the Stokes-flow limit and assess the role of solute advection, characterised by the Rayleigh number. For a purely diffusive salt transport, the velocity field attains an orientation-dependent non-decaying profile at large distances from the sphere, in contradiction to the fundamental requirement of velocity attenuation. title: Surface‐Constrained Reconstruction of Spatiotemporal Turbulence Dissipation in the Convective Boundary Layer Using Physics‐Guided Machine Learning
abstract: Abstract Turbulence dissipation rate (EDR) governs the conversion of turbulent kinetic energy to heat and thereby controls vertical mixing, transport, and energy exchange in the convective boundary layer (CBL). The spatiotemporal structure of EDR remains poorly constrained, as observations are limited to point measurements or sparse vertical profiles that cannot resolve spatiotemporal evolution, hindering evaluation of planetary boundary layer (PBL) parameterizations that rely on simplified turbulence representations. Here we develop a surface‐constrained framework that reconstructs CBL EDR structure from routine surface observations by integrating mixed‐layer physical constraints with a machine‐learning mapping trained on Doppler‐lidar–retrieved EDR at the ARM SGP site. title: Retrieval of Sea Fog Top Height Over the Yellow and Bohai Seas Using Island Elevation
abstract: Abstract Sea fog strongly affects marine transportation and offshore operations, yet its vertical extent remains difficult to determine over broad ocean areas. Active remote sensing can provide accurate vertical information, but its narrow sampling and low temporal resolution make it unsuitable for continuous, large‐scale monitoring of sea fog top height (SFTH). Existing widely used passive satellite cloud top height (CTH) retrieval methods are not well suited to shallow sea fog. Focusing on the Yellow and Bohai Seas, we present a daytime MODIS‐based method for retrieving SFTH by deriving a linear relationship between sea fog reflectance and SFTH, constrained by island peak elevation. title: HTAP3-OPNS: ozone, PM, nitrogen and sulphur deposition – multi-model experiments to support the revision of the CLRTAP Gothenburg Protocol
abstract: HTAP3-OPNS is a multi-model exercise designed to support the revision of the Gothenburg Protocol under the UNECE Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution (CLRTAP). Using an ensemble of Chemical Transport Models (CTMs) and Chemistry-Climate Models (CCMs), this study investigates the long-range transport and impacts of ground-level ozone, particulate matter (PM), and nitrogen and sulphur deposition across different global regions. The project aims to assess the contributions of regional versus extra-regional emission sources, evaluate the suitability of current models, and project changes in air pollution under future emission scenarios and climate conditions. title: Global Multi‐Model Eddy Dissipation Rate Probability Density Functions for Clear‐Air Turbulence Under Climate Change
abstract: Abstract Atmospheric turbulence poses a major risk to aviation, and it is expected to intensify as a response to climate change. The probability density functions (PDFs) of dozens of different clear‐air turbulence (CAT) diagnostics have been found to shift to higher values in response to climate change, consistent with strengthened vertical wind shear at cruising altitudes. The response of the PDF of the eddy dissipation rate (EDR), which is the internationally endorsed measure of turbulence strength, has not previously been studied, however. This study aims to quantify the impacts of these changes in the upper–tropospheric and lower–stratospheric dynamics on global CAT by 2100. title: Combined Assimilation of Radar and AWS Data From Mesoscale Networks for the Record‐Breaking Heavy Rainfall in China
abstract: Abstract Radar data assimilation (DA) alone remains insufficient for precipitation forecasts due to the lack of thermodynamic information in the pre‐storm environment. This study investigates the assimilation of dense automatic weather station (AWS) observations from China's mesoscale network alongside radar during an extreme rainfall event caused by the remnant vortex of typhoon Haikui. Optimal sequence and scale representation of dense AWS observations within the operational two‐step DA framework are examined. Results demonstrate that adding regional AWS data to radar and national‐level observations significantly refines surface wind, temperature, and humidity analyses, directly enhancing precipitation forecasts. Notably, assimilating synoptic‐scale information followed by radar outperfo…
authors: Haiqin Chen, Kun Zhao, Xinyu Zhang, Hao Huang et al.

title: Characteristics, Mechanisms, and Rainfall Impacts of Warm‐Season Boundary‐Layer Jets in the Dongting‐Poyang Lake Region, South of the Middle Reach of the Yangtze River, China
abstract: Abstract Boundary‐layer (BL) jets (BLJs) exhibit significant diurnal variations and can strongly influence precipitation. The Dongting‐Poyang Lake region of China experiences frequent BLJs and heavy rainfall, yet systematic studies remain limited. This study investigates southerly and northeasterly BLJs (SBLJs and NEBLJs) in the region, focusing on their spatiotemporal distributions, formation, and precipitation impacts. SBLJs occur most frequently in summer, characterized by strong, deep south–southwesterly flows with warm advection. SBLJs peak around 02:00 Beijing Time (BJT) and weaken after sunrise as the mixed BL develops, with a typical duration of 1–9 hr. title: Modulation of the Stratospheric Polar Vortex on the Precipitation Dipole Mode in Southeast China During Early‐to‐Mid Winter
abstract: Abstract In this study, we investigated the linkage between the stratospheric polar vortex (SPV) and precipitation in early and mid winter (November–January; NDJ) in Southeast China, using station observations and reanalysis data sets, and verified the linkage using numerical stratospheric nudging model experiments. The results reveal that the SPV has a weak influence on the first empirical orthogonal function (EOF1) mode of precipitation over Southeast China on the interannual timescale, while the second mode (EOF2) characterized by a dipole pattern is related to the strength of SPV with a max 0.49 correlation coefficient. title: Frequency synchronisation and modal mapping of wake dynamics to the performance of a vertical-axis turbine
abstract: The transition towards sustainable marine energy relies partly on efficient deployment of vertical-axis tidal turbines, yet their widespread application is constrained by the complex, unsteady fluid dynamics inherent in their operation. While vertical-axis turbines offer superior structural scalability, they experience intricate vortex shedding and wake-induced energy losses which can make performance difficult to predict accurately. We address this critical gap by establishing a novel, data-driven quantitative correlation between wake characteristics and hydrodynamic performance. A high-fidelity actuator line model within a large eddy simulation framework is used to simulate the three-dimensional dynamic response of a vertical-axis tidal turbine in unsteady flow. title: Turbulent boundary layers under adverse pressure gradients. Part 2. A composite mean velocity profile
abstract: A robust composite mean velocity profile is developed for turbulent boundary layers (TBLs) subjected to adverse pressure gradients (APGs), extending the composite formulation for generic pressure-gradient TBLs proposed by Nickels (2004 J. Fluid Mech. , vol. 521). Several modifications are introduced to capture characteristic features of these APG flows. title: Darcy porous convection with a Jeffreys heat model
abstract: We develop and analyse a theory for thermal convection in a Darcy porous material when the heat transfer is based on a Jeffreys theory. The memory terms in the Jeffreys heat constitutive law lead to the important result that the structure of the instability hinges on the relative size of two non-dimensional parameters, the Maxwell coefficient and the Jeffreys coefficient. This leads to a fundamentally different theory of thermal convection in a porous material. When the Jeffreys parameter is greater than or equal to the Maxwell one we show the linear operator attached to the stability problem is symmetric and instability will only arise via stationary convection. title: Spatial symmetry invariance of three-dimensional Navier–Stokes turbulence
abstract: Direct numerical simulation (DNS) of the deterministic Navier–Stokes (NS) equations is widely used to provide benchmark solutions of turbulent flow, but its accuracy and reliability have not been rigorously inspected from a mathematical viewpoint. Here, we prove a spatial symmetry invariance theorem (SSIT) of three-dimensional NS equations whereby an exact solution of deterministic NS equations under periodic boundary conditions maintains the same spatial symmetry as its symmetric initial flow, forever. SSIT provides an absolute benchmark test for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). It is shown herein that traditional DNS of NS turbulence quickly violates SSIT, revealing that the spatiotemporal trajectory of NS turbulence predicted by DNS soon becomes badly polluted by numerical noise. title: Nonlinear electrophoresis of a dielectric particle in a non-polar media. Part I. Intermediate Debye numbers
abstract: The electrophoresis of a charged dielectric particle in a low conductivity non-polar media is numerically investigated over a wide range of parameters. Association/dissociation reactions that may alter the concentration of free charge carriers in weak non-polar media are not included in the present model. The results are compared with previously published experimental data, revealing a universal relaxation behaviour of the ionic cloud. We describe an electrophoretic regime observed at intermediate Debye numbers and relatively high Dukhin numbers. In this regime, non-equilibrium effects become important and the Smoluchowski formula is no longer applicable. Two charged layers with high tangential fluxes of counterions and coions are identified. title: Improved Estimates of Equilibrium Climate Sensitivity From Non‐Equilibrated Climate Simulations
abstract: Abstract Calculating equilibrium climate sensitivity (ECS) requires simulations of a thousand years or more for the climate to re‐establish equilibrium, but most ECS estimates are derived from shorter model integrations. The widely used “Gregory method” for such estimates systematically underestimates ECS, a bias previously attributed to the time‐dependence of climate feedbacks. Here we demonstrate this underestimate instead arises primarily from an underestimate of radiative forcing. We present a modified method that corrects for the underestimate in forcing, producing ECS estimates that closely align with results from “long‐run” millennium‐scale simulations. This method is robust across models and offers an easily obtainable estimate of ECS with significantly higher accuracy. It enables …

title: Development and validation of ARMS-gb v2.0: extending fast radiative transfer modeling capability to all-sky conditions  for ground-based microwave radiometer retrievals
abstract: Ground-based microwave radiometers provide continuous, all-weather observations of boundary-layer temperature and humidity, closing a critical near-surface observation gap. The Advanced Radiative Transfer Modeling System – ground-based (ARMS-gb) is a fast radiative transfer model specifically designed to simulate the brightness temperatures observed by these instruments. This paper presents ARMS-gb v2.0, which introduces a hydrometeor absorption and scattering module and an accelerated discrete ordinate method (ADOM) solver for multiple scattering. The model now simulates cloud water, rain, ice, snow, and graupel using optical-property look-up tables computed with Mie theory and the discrete dipole approximation (DDA). title: Influence of Particle Properties and Grain Size on Aggregation in Dry Particle‐Laden Volcanic Jets
abstract: Abstract Explosive volcanic eruptions can inject large amounts of ash into the atmosphere. These suspended particles pose hazards to aircraft, so a better understanding of the ash residence time and transport distance is needed. Fine particles combine to form larger aggregates, altering their settling behavior. Ash aggregation is influenced by liquid bonding, electrostatic forces, and preferential concentration driven by turbulence. We examine particle aggregation through controlled, low‐humidity experiments at similar particle‐fluid scaling to conditions near a volcanic vent. title: Dust Aerosol Effects on Charge Structure and Lightning Activity of a Continental Thunderstorm: A Modeling Study With Thompson‐Electrification Scheme
abstract: Abstract A mesoscale electrification‐coupled model was established within the WRF model by integrating with the Thompson microphysics scheme. Based on the Thompson‐electrification scheme and MERRA‐2 aerosol reanalysis data, this study investigated the individual and synergistic impacts of dust aerosols acting as cloud condensation nuclei (cloud condensation nuclei (CCN)) and ice nuclei (IN) on microphysics, charge structures and lightning activity of a rare dust‐associated continental thunderstorm. By four sensitivity experiments, the results demonstrated that elevated CCN concentrations increased the mass content and number concentrations of cloud droplets, whereas high IN significantly amplified ice crystal and snow aggregates concentrations. title: Three-dimensional experimental investigation of the interaction between a rising bubble and a vortex ring
abstract: The interaction between turbulent flows and bubbles is a complex phenomenon ubiquitous in natural and industrial settings. In this work, we experimentally investigate, from a fundamental perspective, the interaction between a rising bubble and a vortex ring in counterflow. Using time-resolved three-dimensional Lagrangian particle tracking (3D-LPT) coupled with shadowgraphy, we obtain simultaneous measurements of the bubble motion and the surrounding liquid flow. This approach enables detailed observation of bubble dynamics, deformation and eventual breakup, as well as the fluid motion. We examine several flow configurations by varying the vortex circulation and the Weber number while maintaining a comparable vortex-to-bubble size ratio. title: Hydrodynamic impact reduction during water entry via a variable damping system
abstract: The extreme impact forces encountered during the early moments of water entry are of critical concern in diverse fields, ranging from spacecraft recovery to aircraft ditching. Herein, we systematically investigate a variable damping strategy that uses an internal non-Newtonian fluid damper to regulate the transmission of impulsive loads during water entry. Through a combined experimental and theoretical approach, the dynamic response of dampers filled with shear-thinning and shear-thickening fluids is characterised. We demonstrate that the peak load transmitted to the main body can be reduced by up to 89.7 % compared to a fully rigid counterpart. title: Meso-NH-ISO v1.0: a water stable isotopologue scheme in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH – application to a 2D West African squall line
abstract: Better understanding how convective processes impact the isotopic composition of atmospheric water has implications for understanding phenomena such as squall lines or tropical cyclones, and for reconstructions of past rainfall extreme events. With this motivation, we implemented water stable isotopologues (HD 16 O and H218O) in the non-hydrostatic mesoscale atmospheric model Meso-NH and its one-moment bulk mixed-phase microphysics scheme. The water stable isotopologues are subject to the same dynamical and physical processes as the light water, but undergo isotopic fractionation during water phase changes. title: Longwave Scattering Effects on Radiative Kernels
abstract: Abstract Longwave (LW) scattering, the redirection of infrared radiation by cloud and aerosol particles, is often neglected in current global climate models (GCMs). However, studies have suggested that LW scattering can influence the Earth's energy budget and climate sensitivity, indicating a need to improve the representation and understanding of this radiative effect. In addition to mean radiative fluxes, LW scattering can also change radiative sensitivities as quantified by radiative kernels. This aspect of the LW scattering effect, especially on the radiative sensitivity of non‐cloud variables, has remained largely unexplored. title: A performance-based multivariable weighting framework  for WRF parameterization-scheme selection
abstract: The selection of physical parameterization schemes is a major source of uncertainty in WRF simulations. A comprehensive evaluation of model performance requires the simultaneous consideration of multiple output variables, but simple multivariable averaging can dilute the influence of variables that are difficult to simulate or that respond strongly to alternative physical-process options. To address this issue, this study proposes a performance-based multivariable weighting framework for WRF parameterization-scheme evaluation. title: CAS FGOALS-f3-L Model Datasets for the Global Emissions Scenario Simulation of the 2°C-Target Aligned with China’s Net-Zero Pathway
abstract: Abstract Achieving net-zero emissions is critical for the 2°C-target set forth by the Paris Agreement. This paper presents a dataset under a sector-specific combined scenario (SSP2-com), which integrates recent national climate commitments, including China’s carbon neutrality pledge. The simulation, performed with the Chinese Academy of Sciences Flexible Global Ocean–Atmosphere–Land System Model, finite-volume version 3 (CAS-FGOALS-f3-L) model, covers 2015–2100 and provides 52 variables at monthly, daily, and sub-daily resolutions, all interpolated onto a 1° × 1° grid. title: Energy transfer and scale organisation in dense canopy turbulence
abstract: This study identifies the scale-dependent processes that sustain turbulence in dense submerged canopy flows. Using a scale-resolved energy budget, we determine where in space and at which scales production, pressure–strain redistribution and inter-scale transfer predominantly occur, and how they link the canopy layer to the overlying shear flow. We show that energy production is localised at the interfacial shear layer, over a narrow range of streamwise and spanwise scales, while fluctuations within the canopy are primarily maintained through inter-scale transfer and pressure–strain redistribution. title: Three-dimensional flutter dynamics of a rectangular plate: Exploring critical conditions and post-critical regimes
abstract: Self-sustained, flow-induced oscillations of a flexible plate have been identified as a viable mechanism for energy harvesting. However, the efficiency of such devices strongly depends on the onset of aeroelastic instabilities. In this work, we investigate numerically the flutter of a rectangular, three-dimensional, inextensible plate invested by a viscous laminar flow. Through a systematic approach, an unprecedentedly broad range of the parametric space spanned by the mass ratio upper M Subscript s M s $M_s$ and bending rigidity upper K Subscript upper B K B $K_B$ is explored. Specifically, three distinct regimes of response can be identified: (i) fixed-point stability, (ii) limit-cycle oscillations and (iii) irregular flutter. title: Instability between shear and surface tension for a thin-film flow surrounding an ellipse
abstract: We consider the thin-film flow of a free-surface fluid surrounding a two-dimensional elliptical substrate. The effects of shear, surface tension, mass injection and varying substrate curvature on the dynamics are modelled in a combined analysis of steady states, linear stability theory and general time-evolution simulations. We discover a symmetry-breaking instability in which the combined effect of surface tension and shear can transport fluid in a direction perpendicular to the shear flow when the elliptical curvature variation is sufficiently large. Symmetric steady solutions are shown to be linearly unstable to asymmetric temporal perturbations, and the resultant instability involves a breaking of symmetry of the fluid surface that arises from the competing effects of shear, surface te…
authors: Josh Shelton, Timothy Frank Peters, Hui Tang, Philippe H. Trinh

title: Comparing inviscid and viscous flows around moving plates
abstract: We compare an inviscid vortex sheet model with continuous leading-edge shedding with direct Navier–Stokes simulations over a wide range of unsteady plate motions at moderate Reynolds number ( italic Re almost equals 1000 Re ≈ 1000 ${\textit{Re}} \approx 1000$ ). Approximately 70 70 $70$ distinct kinematic configurations are examined, spanning both body-dominated and flow-dominated regimes. In body-dominated motions, where the fluid dynamics are primarily driven by prescribed plate accelerations, the inviscid model accurately reproduces normal force histories and the qualitative structure of the induced vorticity field. title: Genetic programming control of quasiperiodic and chaotic oscillations in a thermoacoustic system
abstract: Self-excited thermoacoustic oscillations remain a key obstacle to low-emission combustion, especially in time-aperiodic regimes where quasiperiodic and chaotic dynamics hinder conventional controller design. We experimentally demonstrate data-driven suppression of such aperiodic thermoacoustic oscillations in a flame-driven Rijke tube using genetic programming (GP). In closed-loop form, the GP-discovered control laws are static nonlinear feedback maps that generate, in real time, actuation commands from a sensor signal. Performance is evaluated by a cost function that penalises both the thermoacoustic amplitude (state cost) and the actuation effort (input cost), enabling efficiency comparisons. We benchmark GP closed-loop control (GCC) against GP open-loop control and conventional open-loo…
authors: Bo Yin, Zhijian Yang, Yu Guan, Stephane Redonnet et al.

title: Generation and degradation mechanisms of near-wall particle streaks
abstract: In wall-bounded turbulent flows, inertial particles can form distinct streaks near the wall. In this work, the theory of Johnson et al. ( J. Fluid Mech. , 2020, vol. 883, A27) for wall-normal distribution of particles is generalised to arbitrary directions to reveal the generation mechanism of particle streaks and the degradation mechanism by shear-induced lift force. The Lagrangian point-particle approach is coupled with direct numerical simulations of a turbulent channel flow to provide reliable data for analyses. Simulation results demonstrate that the shear-induced lift force can remarkably reduce the near-wall particle concentration and the degree of particle streaking. Through theoretical analysis, it is found that the generalised turbophoresis effect plays a prominent role in both n…
authors: Lei Shi, Xiaodong Gong, Zheng Gong, Wei Gao et al.

title: A Machine Learning Framework for Objective Definition and Projection of Meteorological Seasons: An Application to the Indian Subcontinent
abstract: Abstract Meteorological seasons are typically defined through fixed calendar intervals or region‐specific thresholds, yet such approaches fail to capture the actual variability of the annual cycle. Here we present a machine learning framework that objectively detects meteorological seasons and projects their future evolution. The method combines Radially Constrained Clustering (RCC) to identify seasons from reanalysis data with a supervised Multinomial Logistic Regression Classifier (MLRC) that allows these definitions to be applied also to climate model projections. We use the Indian subcontinent as a detailed proof of concept region since it has established operational references for monsoon onset and withdrawal, and it includes contrasting seasonal regimes, from monsoon dominated lowlan…

abstract: A sustained drag reduction rate upper R greater than 28 percent sign R > 28 % $R\gt 28\,\%$ (with net power saving greater than 26 percent sign > 26 % $\gt 26\,\%$ ) is obtained for turbulent channels at a series of Reynolds numbers (i.e. italic Re Subscript tau Baseline equals 180 Re τ = 180 $\textit{Re}_\tau =180$ , 395 395 $395$ , 550 550 $550$ ) via a composite drag control (CDC). title: Control of axial dispersion in polymeric flows: Magnetic effect versus electro-osmotic effect
abstract: Since Taylor’s seminal work on the dispersion of soluble matter, the modelling and control of solute dispersion have received considerable attention. This study investigates the solute dispersion in polymer solutions driven by unsteady magnetohydrodynamic (MHD)-oscillatory electro-osmotic flow within a microtube, aiming to reveal the transport mechanisms in complex rheological media through microscale flow. Firstly, based on the Debye–Hückel approximation, analytical solutions for the electric potential and velocity distributions of mixed MHD-electrohydrodynamic flows are rigorously derived. title: Shoaling of internal solitary waves over linear slopes with variable topography
abstract: This study investigates the influence of variable topography on the kinematics of internal solitary wave shoaling across various breaking regimes under the unifying condition of a slope-intersecting pycnocline. It is demonstrated that bottom corrugations can significantly modify the dynamics: in plunging, collapsing and fission cases, variable topography alters wave shape and induces Kelvin–Helmholtz billows within the pycnocline; in surging scenarios, it impedes upslope propagation and generates a reflected mode-2 wave offshore. title: Stratospheric Aerosol From Above: Laser‐Ablation Mass Spectrometer Samples Polar Vortex Air for the First Time
abstract: Abstract The JGR paper by Lawler et al. (2025, https://doi.org/10.1029/2025jd043530 ) marks a significant and historic first, the PALMS single‐particle chemical analysis sampling deep stratospheric Arctic vortex air for the first time. The analysis finds ∼90% of sulfate aerosol particles in the deepest stratosphere air (100–130 ppb N 2 O) are meteoric‐sulfuric particles, their composition spectra having metal cation peaks strongly indicative of meteoric origin (see Figure 2 of Lawler et al., 2025, https://doi.org/10.1029/2025jd043530 ). title: Inter‐Comparison of Snow Depth Over Antarctic Sea Ice From Ocean Reanalyzes and Observations
abstract: Abstract Snow depth on Antarctic sea ice is a critical climate variable affecting energy and mass balance, yet its observation and modeling remain challenging. We present a systematic intercomparison of snow depth from six ocean reanalysis products, two satellite retrievals, and ship‐based and airborne observational constraints. Results indicate that reanalysis and satellite products show consistent large‐scale climatological snow depth patterns, with the highest depths in the Weddell Sea. However, substantial differences remain in magnitude, seasonal phasing, spatial variability, and trends. The multi‐model mean agrees with satellite‐derived products in some integrated metrics, but tends to smooth regional features and may reflect compensation among reanalysis members. title: High-performance geodynamics on GPUs using  the PETSc CUDA backend (GAUZZ v1.0.0)
abstract: GPUs provide much higher memory bandwidth than CPUs. Data-parallel computations with regular memory access patterns exploit the GPU architecture efficiently. To solve the Stokes equations, we apply a preconditioned conjugate-gradient (PCG) method to the Schur complement system. The algorithm is dominated by sparse matrix-vector products, vector inner products, vector updates, and repeated velocity subproblem solves, all of which map onto GPU architectures. We implement the solver in GAUZZ v1.0.0 on GPUs by coupling CUDA-enabled PETSc with FEniCS. PETSc AIJCUSPARSE matrices with CUDA vectors keep operators and field vectors resident in VRAM, which limits CPU-GPU transfers. title: Climatology of Atmospheric Boundary Layer Height Over Nearshore and Open Ocean Regions of the Western North Pacific
abstract: Abstract Atmospheric boundary layer height (ABLH) plays an important role in air–sea interactions and regional climate over the western North Pacific (WNP). Using ERA5 reanalysis data from 1979 to 2025, this paper investigates the interannual variability, monthly variations, and seasonal spatial patterns of ABLH. To explore potential drivers of ABLH variability, correlation analyses are conducted between ABLH and three key predictors: wind shear, surface sensible heat flux (HFX) and Brunt–Väisälä frequency ( N 2 ). In addition, records from nearshore (NS) and open ocean (OS) stations are analyzed to examine spatial differences in ABLH behavior. The results reveal clear regional differences. title: Evaluating Statistical Downscaling Techniques for Regional Hydroclimatic Change Projections Over CONUS
abstract: Abstract Projecting the impacts of future climate change is critical for water managers planning infrastructure resilience strategies. Global earth system model output is generally too coarse to provide the detailed, localized information needed for impact assessment, and the computational cost of running higher‐resolution global simulations over sufficiently long periods is prohibitive. Downscaling methods span a wide range of computational cost, and statistical approaches in particular offer a relatively inexpensive way to refine climate model output into a more actionable form. Here, we assess a broad suite of statistical and simplified dynamic downscaling approaches for nine regions across the coterminous United States (CONUS). We develop a suite of metrics to evaluate these methods, i…

title: Aerosol Retrieval Over Ocean From DPC‐2/GF‐5(02): Using RemoTAP Extended With a 3‐Parameter Ocean Bio‐Optical Model and Comparisons With a 1‐Parameter Model
abstract: Abstract Multi‐angle polarimetric instruments (MAPs) enable the retrieval of essential aerosol properties over oceanic regions. MAPs retrieval algorithms commonly use a 1‐parameter ocean bio‐optical model (OBM), based on chlorophyll‐a concentration only to represent optical properties over open waters (case‐1), whereas the coastal water (mixture of case‐1 and case‐2 waters) representation generally requires multi‐parameter models as demonstrated for sophisticated sensors such as SPEXone. In this study, we investigated whether meaningful improvements in aerosol retrieval over coastal waters can be achieved using data from the Directional Polarization Camera DPC‐2, with a relatively limited spectral configuration, by the addition of bio‐optical degrees of freedom. title: Physics vs. AI in weather prediction: evaluating GraphCast, AIFS, and FuXi against an observation-corrected WRF model for flash floods
abstract: Data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) weather models are increasingly positioned as alternatives or complements to physics-based numerical weather prediction (NWP) systems, yet systematic model evaluation studies that compare both paradigms under controlled experimental conditions remain limited. Here we present a structured model evaluation framework applying standardised verification metrics to assess a regional WRF configuration against three publicly available AI models – GraphCast, AIFS Single 1.0, and FuXi – over three high-impact flood events in Luxembourg and the Greater Region (2016, 2018, and 2021), comprising around 90 simulated days per configuration and 92 119 matched forecast–observation pairs at a four-country network of 259 to 280 stations per event, each screened to be …

title: Enhancing the advection module performance in the EPICC-Model V1.6.0 via GPU-HADVPPM4HIP V1.0 coupling and GPU-optimized strategies
abstract: The rapid development of Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) has established new computational paradigms for enhancing air quality modeling efficiency. In this study, the heterogeneous-compute interface for portability (HIP) was implemented to parallel computing of the piecewise parabolic method (PPM) advection solver (HADVPPM) on China's domestic GPU-like accelerators (GPU-like), resulting in a GPU-accelerated version denoted as GPU-HADVPPM4HIP V1.0. Computational performance was enhanced through three strategic optimizations: reducing the central processing unit (CPU) and GPU (CPU-GPU) data transfer frequency, thread-block coordinated indexing, and the Message Passing Interface (MPI) and HIP (“MPI+HIP”) hybrid parallelization across heterogeneous computing clusters. title: Towards high-fidelity simulations of coastal submesoscale  baroclinic instabilities with MPAS–O (vE3SM3.0.0)  – Part 2: Realistic experiments
abstract: River plumes can strongly influence coastal dynamics but are poorly represented in global ocean models due to stringent resolution requirements. Following the idealized simulations presented in a companion paper (Hinson et al., 2026), this study presents submesoscale-permitting realistic simulations using unprecedented regional refinement with MPAS–O. We assess MPAS–O's ability to represent river plume dynamics by comparing with a validated ROMS configuration focused on the Mississippi–Atchafalaya (M–A) plume in the northern Gulf of Mexico (GoM). The variable-resolution mesh spans 1.4 km in the GoM to 100 km in the Pacific and Indian Oceans. title: An analytical model for rotors in confined flow across operating regimes
abstract: Rotors operating in confined flows, or blockage, are commonly encountered in wind and water tunnels, as well as in shallow or dense deployments of hydrokinetic turbines. Confinement induces a streamwise pressure gradient in the channel, modifying the rotor induction, thrust and power. To account for these effects, physics-based or empirical blockage corrections are used as a transfer function between the dynamics of an object operating in confined and unconfined settings. However, existing blockage models are largely only applicable to rotors operating at relatively low thrust coefficients, such that the assumptions of classical momentum theory are valid. title: Supersaturation Fluctuation Modulates Warm Rain Formation in Cumulus Clouds: Implications for Hygroscopic Cloud Seeding
abstract: Abstract Recent observational studies have demonstrated that supersaturation fluctuations (SS’) in clouds induced by turbulence at scales smaller than 100 m can significantly affect microphysical processes such as aerosol activation and droplet condensation. However, subgrid‐scale SS’ is often ignored in the current model. To investigate the impact of SS’ on warm rain and hygroscopic cloud seeding, this study conducted numerical experiments using the Weather Research and Forecasting large‐eddy simulations for an isolated cumulus cloud in a relatively clean environment. Subgrid‐scale SS’ is represented by Gaussian probability distribution functions. title: How Can the Latent Heat Entrainment Flux in the Convective Boundary Layer be Characterized?
abstract: Abstract A proposed theoretical description of the latent heat entrainment flux at the top of a convective boundary layer (CBL) was tested. It is related to the vertical velocity scale times the ratio of the water vapor mixing ratio (WVMR) gradient to the Brunt‐Väisälä frequency. This relation was tested with different LiDAR and radiosonde measurements. Utilized were observations from several months between 2017 and 2019 from the Atmospheric Radiation Measurement Program's Southern Great Plains site. Water vapor mixing ratio and vertical wind data were retrieved from turbulence‐resolving LiDAR systems, while temperature data were obtained by interpolating radiosonde profiles onto a height grid normalized by the boundary layer height. title: Super Warm Early Eocene Simulations With HadGEM3‐GC31‐LL
abstract: Abstract The early Eocene Climatic Optimum (EECO; 53.3–49.1 million years ago) represents the period of greatest sustained warmth in the Cenozoic (last 66 million years), with proxy‐data indicating global‐mean temperatures 10–16°C above preindustrial and atmospheric concentrations of 1,200–2,500 ppmv. This extreme greenhouse climate provides insights into Earth's climate sensitivity and feedback mechanisms and offers a stress‐test for evaluating climate models under vastly different boundary conditions. Here we present the first application of the HadGEM3‐GC31‐LL model to the super‐warm EECO. title: Surface Nucleation‐Mode Particles Increase During Intense Vertical Exchange Between the Atmospheric Boundary Layer and the Free Troposphere
abstract: Abstract Vertical exchange between the atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) and the free troposphere (FT) is a key pathway for aerosol transport and can substantially influence surface air quality. In this study, an intense ABL‐FT exchange event over Shanghai on 29 March 2024 was captured and analyzed using ground‐based Doppler wind LiDAR, microwave radiometer, particle‐size spectrometer measurements, and numerical diagnostics. Southwesterly warm‐moist advection and daytime surface heating promoted the growth of a warm and moist boundary layer, while drier and more stably stratified air persisted above the ABL top. title: Quantifying Temperature‐Driven Surface Ozone Formation: Insights From Field Observations
abstract: Abstract Tropospheric ozone (O 3 ) pollution has emerged as an increasingly prominent environmental challenge, especially in the context of global warming. This study quantitatively assessed key factors influencing O 3 formation using field observations in cities spanning from northern to southern China and eastern China (Beijing, Haikou, and Suzhou) combined with an interpretable XGBoost‐SHAP model. Model performance was validated across space and time. Temperature explained 33.6% of the total model‐attributed importance for O 3 in Beijing, with effects varying by pollution scenario: highest under co‐pollution (83.3 ± 39.9 μg m −3 , 56%), followed by O 3 pollution (51.9 ± 30.6 μg m −3 , 49%), and PM 2.5 pollution (21.3 ± 11.3 μg m −3 , 25%). title: Evaluating the EPICC-Model for regional air quality simulation: a comparative study with CAMx and CMAQ
abstract: This study presents a systematic evaluation of the EPICC-Model developed in China for regional PM 2.5 and MDA8 O 3 simulations against established international models, using WRF meteorological fields and a multi-source integrated emission inventory. Results highlight the strengths of the EPICC-Model in several aspects: it achieves relatively high spatial consistency with measurements for PM 2.5 , with an annual index of agreement (IOA) of 0.80, and accurately captures pollution patterns in heavily polluted North China. It also demonstrates improved performance in simulating summer O 3 peaks, reducing maximum bias by more than 20 µg m −3 ; this performance may be partly associated with its inclusion of heterogeneous HONO formation and particulate nitrate photolysis. title: Process-based evaluation of green roof models for assessment of heat mitigation efficacy in WRF (v4.3.1) and EnergyPlus (v8.6.0)
abstract: Green roofs mitigate urban heat, but to fully assess their impact, green roof models must be integrated into urban climate models, where they provide critical surface boundary conditions. Ensuring their reliability requires evaluation, yet such efforts remain limited in the literature. This study addresses that gap by evaluating two configurations of EcoRoof, the green roof module from EnergyPlus (ER o for the original version of the model, and ER m for a modified version), and a multilayer green roof parametrization for WRF (WRF-MLGR) (Heusinger et al., 2018; Sailor, 2008; Zonato et al., 2021). title: The weakly nonlinear admittance at open ends of two- and three-dimensional acoustic waveguides
abstract: We formulate a weakly nonlinear exit condition for open ends of acoustic waveguides; to our knowledge, this is the first time a general acoustic open end has been analysed outside the linear regime. The formulation neglects mean flow, vortex separation and viscous effects. title: Beyond classical similitude: group theoretic extrapolation of hypersonic stagnation-point boundary layers
abstract: Motivated by the need to extrapolate the results from ground-based experiments to the conditions of high-speed flight, we present the Lie equivalence-symmetry analysis of the hypersonic stagnation-point boundary layers (BLs). We demonstrate the application of the equivalence symmetry on the set of coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs) which are physically relevant in hypersonics. By allowing the property laws to transform along with the independent and dependent variables, the invariants derived within the similarity-reduced stagnation-point ODE formulation identify families of nonlinear maps that can be used to extrapolate the laboratory-scale predictions to flight. title: The motion of intruders through soft solids
abstract: We present the results of an experimental investigation into the motion of large buoyant rigid spheres rising through highly concentrated collections of hydrated hydrogel particles. The concentration of the soft highly poroelastic particles is such that the mechanical properties of the material are that of a soft solid that can also flow very slowly. Despite the established time-dependent, non-Newtonian character of hydrogel packings, we find that when the upper surface of the material is free, an immersed buoyant sphere travels through the material at a constant speed. Qualitatively distinct behaviour is found when a rigid lid is placed on the surface of the material. In these cases, sublinear time-dependent motion of the sphere is found. title: The emergence of a shock-driven global mode in a confined supersonic channel: beyond Rayleigh flow
abstract: This study identifies a low-frequency, shock-dominated global mode orchestrating thermal choking in confined supersonic flow. The mode exhibits spatial coherence and a bidirectional acoustic–convective feedback loop. Its existence is confirmed – and its inviscid core isolated – through a controlled computational two-dimensional experiment, then validated in fully three-dimensional simulations. Crucially, comparison with one-dimensional Rayleigh flow reveals that choking occurs at a significantly lower heat addition than theoretically predicted, underscoring the dominance of multi-dimensional, mechanically driven choking mechanisms over purely thermal limits. title: Detachment of the trailing-edge vortex from a flat plate that moves impulsively in a fluid
abstract: Two distinct regimes arise during the early development of flow near the trailing edge of a flat plate impulsively started at small angles of attack. The first regime concerns the self-similar growth of a starting vortex at the edge; the second regime involves the advection of the starting vortex away from the edge, as described by Wagner’s classical model, which omits the first regime. In this work, we investigate the transition between these two regimes using a computational inviscid vortex-sheet method and an analytical point-vortex model. title: A physics-guided Fourier neural operator to predict wind-driven water film/rivulet flows pertinent to aircraft icing phenomena
abstract: Aircraft icing poses a critical threat to aviation safety in cold climates, with the dynamic glaze ice accretion process governed by the transient behaviour of wind-driven runback water film and rivulet (WDRWF/R) flows on wing surfaces. Despite its significance, accurately modelling this complex multiphase flow phenomenon remains a fundamental challenge for conventional numerical and theoretical approaches. This study introduces a physics-guided Fourier neural operator (PGFNO) that achieves unprecedented accuracy in predicting the spatiotemporal evolution of WDRWF/R flows relevant to aircraft icing.
